title: Theo and the Ledger
premise: Beatrix Sandoval knows every route, fare, and secret in the town of Harrow Bend — until a cab she dispatched picks up a passenger who vanishes mid-ride, leaving behind the diary of Marisol Vega, a woman missing for three years. The diary's final entries are dated after her disappearance, written in handwriting Beatrix slowly recognizes as her own late father's. Following the ledger of coded fares her father kept as the company's accountant, Beatrix uncovers that Harrow Bend's most respected families used the taxi service to move people — and evidence — out of sight. In the end, Beatrix must choose between protecting the loyal drivers who shielded her father and exposing the truth: Marisol is alive, hidden by her father to protect her, and the diary was his confession meant for Beatrix all along.
about_author: Wren Galloway spent a decade answering phones at a small-town transit depot before turning those overheard lives into fiction. They write mysteries about ordinary workers who know too much.

chapters.title: The Last Fare
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. A routine night shift ends when driver Odell radios in that his passenger, an elderly man, stepped out at the old cannery and never came back — leaving a leather diary on the seat. The name inside belongs to Marisol Vega, missing since 2019. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional calm; Beatrix files the diary instead of calling police, a small act of loyalty that becomes a trap.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Reading the diary at dawn, she finds entries dated months after Marisol vanished — describing the town from hiding, and mentioning 'the ledger' and someone called B. She cross-checks dispatch logs and realizes the final entry references her own father, dead two years. Emotional beat: grief cracking open into suspicion; the closed case reopens inside her chest.

chapters.title: Harrow Bend Keeps Its Books
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, with a flashback interlude in her father's voice via ledger notes. She breaks into the company archive and finds her father's coded fare book: routes marked with symbols matching dates when townspeople disappeared or scandals died quietly. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering your childhood home was a machine; loyalty to her father's memory begins to curdle.

chapters.title: The Drivers' Code
chapters.summary: Odell's POV. The veteran drivers close ranks, warning Beatrix off with ritual phrases her father apparently taught them. Odell reveals only that the code exists to protect 'passengers who need to be unfindable.' Emotional beat: warmth and menace braided together — the men who taught her to drive are also gatekeepers of something terrible.

chapters.title: What the Mayor Paid For
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Following a ledger symbol to a lake house, she finds receipts linking Councilman Aldous Pike to three 'unfindable' fares — including one the night Marisol disappeared. Someone searches her apartment while she's out; the diary is nearly taken. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into purpose; she stops being an investigator and becomes a target.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Dispatch goes dark — her access revoked, her shifts reassigned, the company circling wagons around Pike. Odell goes missing after agreeing to meet her. Emotional beat: isolation and betrayal; the institution that raised her is erasing her, and she understands how Marisol must have felt.

chapters.title: The Cannery Floor
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Decoding her father's final ledger page, she maps a hidden room beneath the derelict cannery where the last fare was logged. Inside: signs of long habitation, fresh food wrappers, and a wall of clippings about her father's death. Emotional beat: dread transforming into revelation — whoever hid here knew him intimately.

chapters.title: A Voice on Channel Four
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV (revealed). Alive, Marisol has been hiding in plain sight, moving between safe houses her father arranged after witnessing Pike arrange a fatal 'accident.' She wrote the post-disappearance diary entries knowing Beatrix would someday inherit the search. Emotional beat: exhausted hope; two inheritances — of secrets and of duty — finally touch.

chapters.title: Closing the Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Pike corners them at the cannery with Odell as reluctant hostage; the confrontation forces the drivers to choose between the code and the truth. Beatrix broadcasts the whole confession over the open dispatch channel so every cab in town hears it. Emotional beat: climax — courage as public witness, loyalty redeemed by truth rather than sacrificed to it.

chapters.title: First Shift
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, weeks later. Pike is arrested, the company under new ownership, Marisol testifying from safety while Odell drives her to the courthouse himself. Beatrix takes the morning shift for the first time in seven years, her father's ledger donated to the county archive. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — the town's secrets are filed, alphabetized, and finally told.
